messages.author: 4e76381869a8beae
messages.subject: Comparing different Disease Mapping methods
parts:
Hello,

I'm interested in conducting a spatial analysis on area-level data. I have all the relevant data and also managed to run a few basic models such as the Poisson-Gamma model or the Log-Normal model.

However, I'm a bit confused regarding evaluation and comparison of results, and couldn't find a good reference to understand how I should compare different models and techniques, as for instance, in predictive-learning classification tasks I would have accuracy, precision, recall etc.

Thanks a lot!
Alan

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Comparing different Disease Mapping methods
parts:
Hi Alan!

What INLA provides you with is the ability to simulate from the posterior, even at locations where you have no data (but want to do predictions).
See inla.posterior.sample

## How to compute the evaluations

However, since INLA is general, you have to implement evaluation criteria yourself (or borrow code from someone who has).

For example: #correct classifications / # total number of data (accuracy??)
- You have to decide how to do point estimates (e.g. posterior mean)
- You have to compute the estimates (summary.fitted values or posterior samples)
- You have to compute the evaluation criteria

## What evaluation criteria to choose for disease mapping

I have worked a bit with modeling a disease in Brazil. However, I have no clear recommendation on what criterion to choose. A major problem I encountered is that diseases have a lot of zeroes and low counts, and prediction criteria may focus on low-counts and high-counts predictions differently.

What I would suggest is a 2-pronged approach

1) Choose criteria which are easy to compute in INLA, like DIC/WAIC/CPO, absence/presence classification, <5 >5 classification, etc.
 - these are not very reliable, but may give you some insight
 - (compare the distribution of the estimates to the distribution of your data (measures of fit))

2) Choose a criteria that represents what you want the end result of your modeling to be. E.g. if you want to predict disease in a large area in one year, you can hold out such subsets of the data and compare the predictive accuracy of the summed disease counts in these held-out sets. This involves running the models 10+ times.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

parts:
Hello Haakon,

Thanks a lot for your detailed answer.

As I need a metric for comparing two models, the ability to predict in places I have no data about is not practical for model fit evaluation.

The basic concept of training-testing like in predictive modeling is less intuitive or possible due to correlations; I wouldn't dare to exclude entire areas! Another idea would be to test for only a few years, but then training and testing differ in time-frames! (and we intend in a future to also look for spatio-temporal effects)

Looking into your suggestions, the idea of holding every year along can be good, but will not be useful when moving into spatio-temporal analysis (and not just spatial)

Regarding easy metrics to compute such as AIC, DIC etc. - are there comparable across non-nested models?

Thanks
Alan

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Comparing different Disease Mapping methods
parts:
When you don't have enough data to leave out a subset of the analysis as a whole to do validation, cross-validation is one of the few general options you have. Leaving out one year at a time would test the ability of the model to predict that year using the past and future years. In some cases, this may be what you want the model to be good at, and then it's an appropriate check. In other cases it's the spatial (and-or spatio-temporal) prediction ability that matters; then you'd just leave out a region at a time, and not the entire year.
So you may need to ask yourself I what _way_ you want the model to be "good", and then target that aspect in the validation checks.  DIC etc can give general hints, but they're very blunt instruments. Targeted posterior predictive checks tend to give more insight.

Finn

Hi Finn

Thanks a lot for sharing your insights. Your comments make sense. 

To be more specific, I'm trying to model the "incidence" of a disease occurring. My data is of 25K patients across ~2500 regions and ~12 years. So in average it is only a patient per year per area, obviously varying with the size of population in every region, and the different disease risks (that is what we are after). I also have a stratification of the population in terms of age etc.

It makes sense to take a leave-one-out approach. I'm a bit worried thought regarding sparsity, but that's completely fixable: I can just take (at random) k = 3 or 4 and average across any evaluation on the k testing sets.

Thanks!
Alan

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Comparing different Disease Mapping methods
parts:
I agree that leaving only 1 out when you have around 1 observation per area*time may not be the best.

Probably, the goal of your analysis is not to be able to predict at a single area*time in the future, but more of an overall abundance?

## Idea / Suggestion
- L5O: Leave 5 out
- Compute the true sum of incidences
- Sample from the posterior and add the samples together for the predicted sum
- Compare the distribution of the predicted sum to the true value of the sum

Why not take the average of the scores for 3-5 different points? I do not think that would give you a proper scoring rule. I think it is better to look at the probability distribution of the sum of the values, and do a proper scoring rule on that target.

## Run time of CV (LOO or L5O)
If you want to run the full Cross-validation, this may take forever. What I would do is to sample points at random to do the prediction scenario on, not sampling the same points twice, and stop when you don't have time to do any more.

## DIC etc
I think these measures often give the wrong answer on what model is best, for your kind of models. One thing you can try is to compute the cpo and look at result$cpo$failures; if the sum of the failures is not too large this gives a very good approximation of the LOOCV. Usually, in your kind of models, there are too many failures.

However, sometimes you get a massive difference in DIC or WAIC, like 10000. That gives you a strong hint that one of the models are better.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

1) Choose criteria which are easy to compute in INLA, like DIC/WAIC/CPO, absence/presence classification, <5 >5 classification, etc.
 - these are not very reliable, but may give you some insight
 - (compare the distribution of the estimates to the distribution of your data (measures of fit))

2) Choose a criteria that represents what you want the end result of your modeling to be. E.g. if you want to predict disease in a large area in one year, you can hold out such subsets of the data and compare the predictive accuracy of the summed disease counts in these held-out sets. This involves running the models 10+ times.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka
